title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
claim: Fixed-horizon multi-step backups are highly sensitive to cap length, while ours keeps a favorable bias-variance balance and stable returns.
layout: 2 scatter panels plus 1 learning-curve panel, left-to-right, shaded concentric markers for cap length
description: The figure has two parts. Part (a) is a pair of scatter plots, one for 100K steps and one for 1M steps. The x-axis is normalized fixed-point bias and the y-axis is empirical variance on a log scale. Each method is shown as a cluster of concentric circles. Darker shades mark shorter caps. Green is MINT, red is Peng, and blue is n-step. At 100K steps the green cluster sits at high bias but low variance, while red and blue sit at low bias and higher variance. At 1M steps the clusters are tightly grouped, and blue has the highest variance. Part (b) shows Hopper learning curves of average return against steps up to 1000K. The green MINT curves rise fast and plateau near 3500 with little spread across caps. The red dashed Peng curves stay near 1000. The blue dash-dotted n-step curves vary widely and have wide shaded bands. A shared legend sits below each part.
caption: Cap-length sensitivity on MuJoCo Hopper (SAC). (a) Bias and variance at $100$K and $1$M steps for caps $\{3,5,10,20\}$ (darker shades indicate shorter caps). MINT exhibits a favorable empirical bias--variance balance across the tested caps; several baseline configurations have higher variance at longer caps. (b) Learning curves for the same caps. MINT attains high returns across the tested values, whereas baseline performance varies more with the cap.
abstract: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.
